slides.headline: NASA hit an asteroid. It left a stadium-sized crater
slides.subline: **Europe’s Hera probe** has just sent the first close-ups, 4 years later.
slides.credit: ESA / Hera, Asteroid Framing Camera / CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO (Didymos and Dimorphos)

slides.body: In 2022 NASA crashed its **DART** spacecraft into a small asteroid called [[Dimorphos]] to see if humans can push a space rock off course. It worked: its orbit got **33 minutes shorter**.
Nobody knew what DART had done to the rock itself. Scientists argued: a **crater**, a **new shape**, or [[no change]] at all?
Hera’s lead scientist says it is [[all three]]. The side DART hit is **flattened into a crater the size of a sports stadium**, spanning the asteroid’s whole width.
Dimorphos is **tumbling wildly** in its orbit since the impact. And **hundreds of boulders**, a few metres wide, are floating around the pair.
Hera moves in to about **13 km** in December. In January it releases two **shoebox-sized** CubeSats. Would you trust a spacecraft to save Earth from an asteroid? Tell us below.
